summary: Round 2, tests only. Both round-1 majors are killed on the current bytes, measured by mutation in an issued tree (302 sequencer tests green at baseline). Round-1 major 1 (recording built from sibling locals): `new Issued(` now appears exactly once, at CommitProtocolSimulation.java:81, inside `record(CommitRequest)` reading only the request's accessors -- reverting ONLY the leader request's flushSeq argument to `commits` now fails BOTH tests (FlushSeqTest:76 and :112) where it was green at round 1. Round-1 major 2 (per-pod unpinned): a single fleet-wide per-attempt counter (constant allocator key) now fails the density test at FlushSeqTest:112. Twelve of thirteen mutations killed; the surviving one is recorded below as a minor and should NOT be fixed this round. Neither test can pass vacuously: dropping the recording entirely fails both on their anti-vacuity guards (:81, :127), and collapsing every pod name to pod0 -- byPod with a single entry -- fails both (:85, :127), because density from 0 plus two issuing pods forces a shared value by construction. Red records are honest: red.log shows the density test red at line 112 (its own density equality, not a compile error and not the sibling's assertion) and the uniqueness test red at line 76 (its own segment-mismatch assertion); the recorded source sha256 matches the staged file byte for byte. No existing assertion was weakened -- the only change to an existing assertion in the diff is the `.as(...)` description on the pods-size guard, the predicate `hasSizeGreaterThan(1)` is unchanged. Tier is right (T1, MemoryBinStore + SimulatedClock, no socket, no sleep, no fixed port, no system temp); @Timeout(120, SEPARATE_THREAD) is present and the pair runs in ~4s.

findings.title: The segmentKey field of the Issued triple is unconstrained: replacing it with a constant survives both tests
findings.mutation: In `record(CommitRequest)`, change `request.segmentKey()` to a literal, e.g. `return new Issued(request.podId(), request.flushSeq(), "seg/constant");`. MEASURED: both tests stay green, BUILD SUCCESSFUL.
findings.failure_scenario: The uniqueness test's core assertion (FlushSeqTest:72-76) only executes when a `(podId, flushSeq)` pair repeats, which never happens once the allocator is correct, so under the fixed harness the third field of the triple is never read. If a later change made the segment recording constant or otherwise unfaithful -- and grep confirms nothing else in the tree reads `Issued.segmentKey()` -- the reissue detector would compare a constant against a constant and report agreement, i.e. it would go blind exactly when a genuine reissue was reintroduced, and the failure would look like a passing test.
findings.why_not_blocking: Low consequence and probably should NOT be fixed this round. The density test does not read segmentKey at all, so every allocator regression I could construct (including the reissue shapes) is still caught at FlushSeqTest:112 independently of this field; the blindness needs TWO simultaneous defects. The structural fix from round 1 -- one `new Issued(` call site reading only the request's accessors -- is what makes the divergence implausible in the first place. Killing it would require a negative control that deliberately reissues a pair and asserts the detector fires, i.e. a test of the harness's detector rather than of the protocol, and that is more surface than the risk warrants.
